text: Paul always dreaded going home to Cordelia Street, where all the houses were exactly alike and businessmen of moderate means raised large families and sent their children to Sunday school. <break time="0.8s" /> He hated the ugly yellow wallpaper of his room, the pictures of George Washington and John Calvin above his bed, and the whole flavor of an ordinary, respectable life. <break time="0.8s" /> That night he could not face his father, so he crept in through a basement window and sat awake until dawn, half afraid that his father would mistake him for a burglar. <break time="0.8s" /> On Sunday afternoons all the people of Cordelia Street sat out on their front steps, and the men talked about prices, promotions, and the legends of the iron kings. <break time="0.8s" /> Pauls father held up as a model a young clerk who worked for a steel magnate and who, on his employers advice, had married early and settled down. <break time="0.8s" /> Paul cared only for the tales of the iron kings, with their palaces in Venice and yachts on the Mediterranean, for the clerks dull virtues meant nothing to him. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening he asked his father for carfare, saying he was going to study geometry with a classmate, and his father gave him the money, warning him not to be out late. <break time="0.8s" /> But Paul went instead to the theater, where his friend Charley Edwards, a young actor in the stock company, let him help in the dressing room and watch the rehearsals.
